ch02.title: Six Choose Six
ch02.b001: The Day They Went Out Two by Two
ch02.b002: On the afternoon of the day he proclaimed the kingdom in the synagogue, Jesus called the six apostles together and began to tell them of his plans for visiting the towns around the Sea of Galilee. He did not call his brothers James and Jude to that meeting. The two of them were deeply hurt. Until then they had counted themselves among his closest circle. But Jesus had already decided that no near kinsman of his would be a member of the apostolic corps of the kingdom. That decision was where a crack first opened between him and his family, and through all his public life the crack only widened. Only Ruth, the youngest, never once left the side of the brother who had been a father to her.
ch02.b003: The next day, Sunday, June 23, A.D. 26, Jesus gave the six their final instructions. They were to go out two by two and teach the glad tidings of the kingdom of heaven, but they were not to baptize and were not to preach in public. Later he would let them preach openly, he said; for now he wanted them first to gain experience in meeting people one at a time. The apostles were a little disappointed. They had not imagined the kingdom would begin so quietly. Still, they packed their things in good heart. The sons of Zebedee would cross the lake to Kheresa, the brothers Andrew and Peter would stay in Capernaum, and Philip and Nathaniel would go south to Tarichea.
ch02.b004: Before they left, Jesus told them one thing more. He meant to ordain twelve apostles who would carry on the work of the kingdom after he was gone, and so each of them was to choose one man from among the early believers and bring him into the apostolic company. John asked a question. They had been with him since the Jordan and had heard all his teaching. Would these six newcomers share everything with them equally? Jesus said yes. The men they chose would become one with them, and they would teach those men everything about the kingdom, just as they themselves had been taught. Then he left them.
ch02.b005: The six talked for a long time. Whom should they choose? Was it really for them to choose at all? In the end it was Andrew’s word that carried. The Master was right, he said; there were too few of them for this work, and if he had trusted them to pick six new apostles themselves, that showed how much confidence he had in them. They set out holding on to that. But each of them carried a weight in some corner of his heart. They would have to go two weeks without him, and they were afraid. Above all, this was not how they had pictured the first day of the kingdom.
ch02.b006: During those two weeks Jesus went over to Nazareth and visited Joseph and Simon and the other members of his family who lived round about. He did everything a man could do to keep the love and trust of his family. And he thought often about John in prison. The temptation to use his power to set John free was strong. But once more he gave himself over to waiting on the Father’s will. The apostles learned of this only much later.
ch02.b008: Just east of Capernaum, on the road that ran toward Batanea, stood the customs house. Matthew Levi sat at its table and counted the goods that went by: baskets of salted fish, jars of oil, bales of wool, cloth coming down from Damascus. He was thirty-one, with a wife and four children. The Levi family had been in business and tax gathering for generations. That was why the household was comfortable. And that was why few men in front of the synagogue ever greeted him first.
ch02.b009: He was good at dealing with people. He could tell in a moment who was lying, who was truly in hard straits, who was polite only on the surface. A tax man who could not read people did not survive. But in the past few days one man kept turning up at his table whom he could not read at all. It was Andrew, the fisherman from Bethsaida. He and his brother Peter were going around the lanes of Capernaum meeting people. He did not shout and he did not stand up in the synagogue. He simply stopped one person at a time and talked with him for a long while.
ch02.b010: The first time he stood before the customs house, Matthew asked whether he had goods to declare. Andrew said no. And then, instead of going on, he sat down. Matthew had never before seen a fisherman sit down of his own accord beside a tax collector’s table.
ch02.b011: “Have you heard about Jesus of Nazareth?”
ch02.b012: Matthew had. No one in the city had not heard that name: the story of the wine at Cana, the strange sermon on the kingdom in the synagogue. He had heard that sermon himself, from the shadow of a pillar at the very back. When the preacher said that in this kingdom no one would be set apart, not Jew or gentile, rich or poor, slave or free, Matthew had stopped breathing for a moment. The word publican was not on that list. But he wanted to know whether the list was wide enough to take in a publican too.
ch02.b013: Andrew came again the next day, and the day after. He did not say a single word of praise. He only listened to everything Matthew said, and seemed to hear even what Matthew did not say. Matthew found, to his surprise, that he liked it. The people he met either wanted something from him or avoided him. This man neither wanted anything nor avoided anything. As the two weeks were ending, Andrew said briefly that he would soon come back with the Master. Matthew understood what that meant. That night he told his wife he would have to settle his books.
ch02.b014: His wife looked at him for a long time and then asked about the children. All four were still small. Matthew told her not to worry. They were well off, and for the first time that wealth felt as if it might be good for something. Even lying in bed he kept doing sums: the share to leave for this house, the share to hand over with the business to his brother, and the share that was left. He did not yet know what he would do with what was left. He knew only that it was money from the customs house, and that to some people it would look like dirty money. That thought kept him awake a long time.
ch02.b016: After two weeks the six came back to the house of Zebedee. They were elated. The first journey had gone far better than they had expected. They had learned in their own bodies how valuable it was to meet people face to face. They had learned that religion was, in the end, a matter of each person’s own experience, and how hungry ordinary people were for words of comfort and good cheer. When they sat down around the Master, they all started talking at once. Peter’s voice was the loudest, and Nathaniel’s story was the longest.
ch02.b017: Andrew raised his hand. One at a time, he said. He had each of them make a formal report to the Master and name the man he was putting forward as a new apostle. So the six names came out. Andrew put forward Matthew Levi, the customs collector of Capernaum. Philip named Thomas Didymus, a fisherman of Tarichea who had once worked as a carpenter and stone mason at Gadara. James Zebedee named James Alpheus, a fisherman and farmer of Kheresa, and John named his twin brother, Judas Alpheus. Peter named Simon, who had been a high officer among the Zealots, and Nathaniel named Judas Iscariot, from Jericho.
ch02.b018: When the tax collector and the Zealot were named side by side, the air in the room went stiff for a moment. Peter wore the face of a man not the least ashamed that his choice was a Zealot, and Andrew made no attempt to explain that his choice was a publican. Andrew thought his brother’s choice was a bold one. He thought it was a good one, too. He wanted to tell his brother so, and once again he could not. He only clapped him once on the back. Peter, puzzled, had no idea why. But no one objected. Jesus had the other five vote on each nomination, and all six names were accepted by everyone. Jesus said they would all go together to call these men. Then he spent the whole of that day with the six, listening to the details of what they had been through and answering their questions. Only now did they understand why the Master had not set them in front of great crowds from the start, but had sent them quietly to meet people one by one.
ch02.b020: The next day Jesus and the six went to the customs house. Matthew was waiting for them. His books were balanced, and everything was ready to be handed over to his brother. That morning he had come out earlier than usual and wiped down the table. His hand shook so that he wiped the same spot three times. When the group appeared at the end of the road, he could not stand up. His legs would not obey him.
ch02.b021: Andrew stepped forward with Jesus. Jesus looked into Matthew’s face and said, Follow me.
ch02.b022: That was all. He did not ask what sins Matthew had committed, or demand to know what he would give up. Matthew searched those eyes for the things he had spent his whole life avoiding: contempt, calculation, grudging generosity. There was nothing of the kind there. The man was looking not at a customs collector but at Matthew. Matthew got to his feet. This time his legs obeyed. He did not look back at the table.
ch02.b023: They went to Matthew’s house. Matthew said, carefully, that he would like to give a banquet that evening. If the Master approved and would be the guest of honor, he wanted to entertain his family and friends. Jesus nodded his consent. Then Peter took Matthew aside, told him that he had invited a man named Simon to join the apostles, and asked whether Simon might be bidden to the feast as well. At the name Matthew hesitated for an instant. There was only one Zealot in Capernaum called Simon. He said yes, of course. He could not have given any other answer. Today he was a man who had been received.
ch02.b025: After the noon meal at Matthew’s house they all followed Peter to call on Simon. Simon was at the shop he used to run, which his nephew now kept. He was twenty-eight and came of a good Capernaum family. He had started out as a merchant, but since throwing himself into the Zealots the business had been left behind. He held a high office among them, among men who believed that any means at all was justified in throwing off the Roman yoke.
ch02.b026: Peter had first come looking for him two weeks earlier. Peter talked a great deal, and Simon talked even more. More than once they had raised their voices. But Simon could not forget that sermon in the synagogue. The man had spoken of a kingdom that would not come with armies. At first Simon had thought it cowardly. But the face that said it was not a coward’s face. It was too calm. It was full of conviction and yet in no hurry at all. Simon had never in his life possessed that kind of composure. He was a man moved by anger, and his anger always ran ahead of him.
ch02.b027: Jesus stood before him, greeted him, and said only, Follow me. Simon decided on the spot. Giving up his office among the Zealots, hearing the curses of his old comrades: those would come afterward. And they did come, soon. Some called him a traitor; some said he had gone mad. Simon told them to wait and see; this man was different. Even he could not have said exactly how. But he had seen that this man was winning people’s hearts, and he believed that whoever won the hearts would in the end win the nation. He gave his nephew a few instructions and left the shop. Then, walking along with the others, he realized where they were going. To the house of Matthew, the tax collector.
ch02.b028: Simon set his teeth. He knew the Levi family. Among the Zealots, tax collectors were worse than gentiles: men who squeezed the blood of their own people and handed it to Rome. Was he to cross the threshold of such a man and eat at such a man’s table? He looked at the back of Jesus walking ahead of him. Jesus went into the house without the slightest hesitation. Simon stood at the door for a moment. Then he went in. It had been less than an hour since he had said he would follow.
ch02.b029: Until the evening meal they talked a good deal about politics and religion. Simon would not meet Matthew’s eyes, and Matthew did not look at Simon. The two sat as far apart as the room allowed. Nathaniel looked from one to the other and whispered in Philip’s ear.
ch02.b030: “If those two ever sit down at one table, the kingdom has already come.”
ch02.b031: Philip bit his lip to keep from laughing.
ch02.b032: The Feast of Publicans and Sinners
ch02.b033: By evening Matthew’s house was full of guests. Most of the people Matthew had invited were men like himself: traders, tax gatherers, people who were not welcome at the synagogue. The Pharisees would have lumped them all together as publicans and sinners. And the Pharisees were in fact there. In those days, when a banquet was given in honor of a well-known man, it was the custom for anyone who was interested to linger about the house, watch the guests at their meal, and listen to the talk. Most of the Pharisees of Capernaum had gathered to see how the Nazarene would conduct himself at this unusual feast.
ch02.b034: As the meal went on, the laughter grew louder. Wine went round, and someone began to sing. Matthew thought about how long it had been since such sounds had been heard in his house. At first his guests held back from Jesus, but they soon saw that he laughed just as they did and tore his bread just as they did, and they relaxed. The faces of the watching Pharisees grew harder and harder.
ch02.b035: As the speeches were beginning, one of the Pharisees came up to Peter and spoke sharply to him. How could they teach that this man was righteous, when he ate with publicans and sinners and sat at so frivolous a gathering? Peter’s face went red. Instead of answering, he whispered the words to Jesus. It was a rare day when Peter held his tongue.
ch02.b036: Before giving his parting blessing, Jesus stood up. He said that in coming here to welcome Matthew and Simon, he was glad to see their lightheartedness and the joy of their fellowship. But they should rejoice still more, because many of them would enter the coming kingdom of the spirit and find better things there. And to those who stood about finding fault with him in their hearts for making merry with these friends, he said that he had come to bring joy to those whom society tramples down and spiritual liberty to those held captive in moral bondage. Need he remind them that it was not the healthy who needed a physician, but the sick? He had not come to call the righteous, but sinners.
ch02.b037: Matthew heard it standing by the door. To call sinners. All his life he had heard that word behind his back: in the market, in front of the synagogue, in the tear-stained faces of his children when they came home from play. Now for the first time the word came at him from the front. Not as a word that exposed his shame, but as a word that opened a door. He looked at the faces of his guests. They too had understood. Matthew turned his head away. He did not want anyone to see his tears. That night he made a decision in his heart: for this man he would give everything he had. He told no one of that vow. Telling no one was part of the vow.
ch02.b038: Simon Zelotes heard the words differently. Joy to the downtrodden, liberty to the captives. His heart pounded. These were the very words he had been shouting all his life. He wanted to stand up. In front of the Pharisees, in front of these publicans and sinners, he wanted to tell them once and for all what freedom was. Just as he began to rise, someone caught him by the elbow. It was Andrew.
ch02.b039: Andrew said a few words in a low voice. The Master did not want the coming kingdom to be confused with the movement of the Zealots. Tonight was for welcoming Matthew and Simon. Simon glared at him. But in Andrew’s eyes there was neither rebuke nor contempt. Slowly Simon sat back down. For the first time he wondered whether the freedom he had meant to speak of and the freedom the Master spoke of were the same thing. That doubt would follow him for a long time.
ch02.b040: That night Jesus and the apostles stayed in Matthew’s house. The guests, going home, spoke of only one thing: how good and how friendly that man had been. It was a rare sight in all Jewry, a man of righteous and noble character mingling freely and gladly with tax collectors and people of bad repute. Matthew saw the last of his guests off and closed the door. Across the yard, in the dark, Simon was standing. For a moment the two men looked at each other. Neither spoke first. Simon was the first to turn his back. But this time he did not spit. Matthew noticed that.
ch02.b041: Lying down, Matthew went back over the day from the beginning: his hand wiping the table that morning, the two words Follow me, and the saying that he had come to call sinners. He wondered what to call this thing he had joined. Kingdom was too big a word, and movement was Simon’s word. After a long while he gave it a name of his own: the business of finding God. Whether you were a tax collector or a Zealot, the one thing that business required was faith. He liked that name. For the rest of his life he would love to speak of it that way.
ch02.b043: The next day the nine of them crossed by boat to Kheresa to call the twin sons of Alpheus, whom James and John Zebedee had chosen. The twins knew they were coming and were waiting on the shore. They waved in exactly the same way, and before the boat touched land they waded out into the water in exactly the same way and took hold of the gunwale. Seeing the two of them, Matthew laughed out loud for the first time.
ch02.b044: James Zebedee presented the Master to the fishermen of Kheresa. Jesus looked at the twins, nodded, and said, Follow me. That afternoon he taught them at length about taking part in festive gatherings. All men were his brothers, he said; the Father in heaven despised no creature. They were not to refuse to break bread with Pharisee or sinner, Sadducee or publican, Roman or Jew, rich or poor; the door of the kingdom stood wide open to everyone who wished to know the truth and find God. At the word Roman, Simon Zelotes frowned; at the word publican, Matthew lowered his eyes.
ch02.b045: That night, at a simple supper in the Alpheus home, the twins were received into the apostolic family. For the first time Jesus taught them about unclean spirits: where they came from, what they were, and what would become of them. None of them understood what he meant. It was easy to love him and admire him. But it was very hard to understand his teaching. The twins were not the least embarrassed at failing to understand. They were happy without understanding. They were twenty-six, and both were married; James had three children and Judas two. All evening the children ran about the yard, and the twins’ wives kept busy filling the strangers’ bowls. James Zebedee watched the commotion and, for once, laughed long. He was a man who went silent for days at a time, but watching the men he had chosen rejoice so simply loosened even his silence.
ch02.b047: After a night’s rest the company, now eleven, went by boat to Tarichea, a small village on the west bank where the Jordan flows out of the Sea of Galilee. Two men were standing at the fishing-boat landing: Thomas the fisherman, and Judas, who had been wandering about in search of work.
ch02.b048: Thomas had been at the landing since morning. He was twenty-nine, with a wife and four children. He had been a carpenter and stone mason, but he had come to this village and become a fisherman, and people looked on him as its leading citizen. Yet no one said he was easy to live with. He doubted everything first. Since losing his twin sister when he was nine, he had come to believe that the world could take away whatever was most precious at any moment. That belief had made him quarrelsome and pessimistic. When Philip first spoke to him of the kingdom, Thomas had picked the story apart point by point. Philip did not give way. As always, he only said, Come and see.
ch02.b049: Beside him stood Judas Iscariot. He was thirty and unmarried. He had been born in Kerioth, a small town in southern Judea, and had grown up in Jericho. He was the only son of wealthy Sadducee parents, and when he followed John the Baptist, they disowned him. He had been about to take work with a fish-drying business at the lower end of the lake, and it was there that he had met Nathaniel. Nathaniel thought highly of his skill with money.
ch02.b050: While they waited for the boat, the two exchanged a few words.
ch02.b051: “Do you believe in all of them?” Thomas asked.
ch02.b052: Judas thought for a moment. “I’m standing here to find out whether they’re worth believing.”
ch02.b053: Thomas liked that answer. Judas added that those men were all Galilean fishermen; he was the only one from Judea. There was pride and loneliness in equal parts in the way he said it. Thomas nodded. He was not a native of this village either. His parents lived in Tiberias, and they had never been happy together. He knew what it felt like to belong nowhere completely. He thought he had met one of his own kind. Later he would learn that he had been wrong. Thomas was standing there to find out; Judas was standing there to calculate.
ch02.b054: The boat came in. Thomas led the party to his house nearby. His wife met the guests at the door. She had already heard that her husband would be spending most of his days away from home with these men. In her face Thomas read relief before he read any sorrow. He did not blame her for it. But he remembered that face for a long time.
ch02.b055: Philip put Thomas forward as his choice for apostle, and Nathaniel put forward Judas. Jesus looked first at Thomas. He told him that he lacked faith. Nevertheless, he said, he received him. Follow me.
ch02.b056: No one in the room breathed. Thomas’s face burned. At their first meeting, and not in some stranger’s house but in his own, with his wife and children looking on, he had been told that his faith was lacking. He looked for a retort. He had done that all his life. But this time no words came. They did not come because what had been said was true. And they did not come because the man who said it had not sent him away. Lacking, and yet received. Thomas could not see how those two things could fit into a single sentence. In the world he knew, what was lacking was thrown out. You did not build with a cracked stone. Yet this man had picked up a cracked stone, knowing it was cracked, and said he would build with it. Thomas bowed his head. That was his answer.
ch02.b057: Then Jesus looked at Judas. We are all of one flesh, he said. In receiving him among them, he prayed that Judas would always be loyal to his Galilean brothers. Follow me.
ch02.b058: Judas bowed deeply. These were words of welcome, he told himself: warm words taking a Judean into a company of Galilean fishermen. That was how he heard them. That was how he chose to hear them. But when he raised his head, a small thorn had lodged in a corner of his heart. I pray that you will be loyal. Why those words, of all words? To Thomas the Master had named what was lacking. What had he named in Judas? Judas tried to work out the answer and then stopped. A sum that would not come out was something he habitually folded away in a corner of the ledger.
ch02.b059: When they had rested and eaten, Jesus took the twelve apart, prayed with them, and taught them about the nature and work of the Holy Spirit. For the most part they did not understand. One grasped this point and another that, but none of them took in the whole. Again and again they tried to fit the new gospel into the old frames of their faith.
ch02.b060: The next day Jesus left the twelve entirely to themselves. He wanted them to get to know one another and to talk over among themselves what he had taught them. It was a harder day than they expected. For the first several hours each of them sat only beside men he already knew: fishermen with fishermen, twin beside twin. Matthew sat alone by the door; Simon stood alone at the window. Judas stayed near Nathaniel, but whenever Nathaniel made a joke he only half laughed.
ch02.b061: Thomas studied them one by one. Those six had known one another a long time. These six did not know one another at all. And in between were a tax collector and a Zealot. Could this group ever truly become one body? He counted up about ten reasons why it could not. Then around midday the twins began grilling the fish they had caught along the shore, and Thomas watched everyone drift, one or two at a time, toward the fire. Simon came, and so did Matthew. They sat facing each other across the flames. They did not speak, but they ate the same fish cooked over the same fire. Thomas crossed one of his ten reasons off the list.
ch02.b062: That afternoon Judas watched Matthew for a long time. Both of them were men who understood money. Judas noted Matthew’s cloth, his sandals, the pale mark of a ring on his finger, and saw that the man owned a good deal. A tax collector’s money. He turned the phrase over in his mind. To a Judean, a tax collector stood even lower than he did to a Galilean. Yet the Master had accepted a feast in that tax collector’s house, and had asked Judas for loyalty. Judas set the two side by side and tried to make them add up. Once again the sum would not come out. He folded it away in the corner of the ledger with the other. Day by day, that folded corner would grow a little thicker.
ch02.b063: The Master came back in time for the evening meal. After supper he spoke to them about the ministry of seraphim, and some of them understood. They rested one more night, and then went back by boat to Capernaum.
ch02.b065: Zebedee and Salome had moved to live with their son David, so that their large house could be given over to Jesus and the twelve apostles. There, for the first time, the twelve spent a quiet Sabbath together. Jesus carefully laid out his plans for proclaiming the kingdom. And he stressed again and again how important it was to avoid any clash with the civil authorities. If the rulers had to be rebuked, he said, they were to leave that to him; they must make no denunciations of Caesar or of Caesar’s servants.
ch02.b066: Hearing this, Simon Zelotes cracked his knuckles one by one. No denunciations of Caesar? But he seized on the words leave that to me. To leave a thing to someone might mean that he would do it himself one day. That was how Simon read it.
ch02.b067: Judas Iscariot heard it too. And that evening, while the others were taking the evening air in the garden, he went up to Jesus and asked whether he might speak with him for a moment. The two withdrew to one side of the garden. Judas brought out a question he had carried for a long time. Why was nothing being done to get John out of prison? Judas had been John’s disciple. For John’s sake he had lost his parents. And now John lay in Herod’s dark prison, while this man who had turned water into wine sat by the Sea of Galilee grilling fish with fishermen.
ch02.b068: Jesus answered him. What that answer was, Judas never told anyone. He knew only that it had not wholly satisfied him. He bowed respectfully and withdrew. Nothing showed on his face; he was good at that. But as he crossed the garden back toward the others, a small voice inside him became distinct for the first time. This man could, and he does not. Why? The voice had not yet reached any conclusion. It had only driven a question mark into his heart. And that question mark would stay there a long time.
ch02.b069: From across the garden Andrew had seen the two of them standing apart. He could not hear what they said. When Judas came back and mingled with the group again, his face was the same as ever. Andrew looked at that face once more. And he said nothing. There was nothing to say yet. That night, in the great house of Zebedee, twelve beds were laid out under one roof for the first time. Matthew and Simon lay at opposite ends of the room, and the twins fell asleep at once, back to back. Thomas stared at the ceiling a long while. The words that his faith was lacking were still in his ears. Yet strangely, they did not hurt him. For the first time someone had measured him exactly, and having read the measure, had not put him down. He did not yet know what that meant. It would take him years to find out. Judas was the last to fall asleep.
ch02.b071: The course of events follows Paper 138, sections 1 to 5. The meeting with the six after the sermon on the kingdom and the exclusion of Jesus’ brothers (138:0.1); the first mission two by two, the announcement of twelve apostles, John’s question, Andrew’s counsel, and Jesus’ visit to Nazareth and his thoughts of John in the meantime (138:1.1–1.5); the reports of the six, their nominations, the vote, and the particulars of the six new apostles (138:2.1–2.10); the calls of Matthew and Simon Zelotes, the banquet at Matthew’s house, the Pharisee’s criticism, Jesus’ reply, and Andrew’s restraint of Simon (138:3.1–3.8); the call of the twins at Kheresa and the teaching of that day (138:4.1–4.4); and the call of Thomas and Judas at Tarichea, the day the twelve were left alone, the Sabbath at Zebedee’s house, and Judas’s question (138:5.1–5.4) are drawn from the text. The ages, families, home towns and characters of the apostles come from Paper 139 (139:7.1–7.4, 139:7.8, 139:8.2–8.3, 139:8.10, 139:9.1, 139:11.1–11.5, 139:12.1–12.2).
ch02.b072: Added as fiction are the inner thoughts and memories of the characters; Andrew’s visits to the customs house during the two weeks; Peter’s earlier meetings with Simon; the whispered exchange between Nathaniel and Philip; Matthew and Simon facing each other in the yard after the feast; the words between Thomas and Judas at the landing; the expression on the face of Thomas’s wife; the fish grilled on the day the twelve were left alone; and small details such as the sleeping arrangements that night. The text does not say what Jesus answered to Judas’s question, so no answer is invented.
ch02.b073: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
